findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. That covers what it is and why it matters in the first screen.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The title and main heading are about firstmate, not Athena. A newcomer at the Athena URL may think the site belongs to firstmate or not know which project is the subject until they read the third paragraph.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title> and the h1 of the same text

findings.text: Nearly all of the page is a detailed state-machine study of firstmate's internals: 12 transition cards, 6 design-choice cards and 45 claims. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena has to scroll past all of it, and nothing says they can skip it.
findings.source: Headings "States of a piece of work", "Counters", "Transitions", "Why it is built this way", "Claims and sources"

findings.text: What to do next is clear. A link in the header jumps to concrete steps: prerequisites, git clone, ./setup.sh and an example `athena ask "add a changelog"` command.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the "Next steps" section

findings.text: "Predictions" is never explained. The page also never shows what Athena's output looks like, such as the traced commit, the cost record or the verdict the header promises. So the newcomer has no example of the main product.
findings.source: "It shows how it read the request and its predictions; press Enter to run it on your repository."

findings.text: This header link speaks to the site's owner, not a visitor. A newcomer won't know what "proposals" or "your decision" mean here.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The page does say the study is a demonstration. But it doesn't say how the study relates to the main promise of turning a short request into a commit, so it's unclear why a study is the first thing shown.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim"

findings.text: The "About this page" section gives an internal repository detail that means nothing to someone who has never seen the repository.
findings.source: "This page's study id, firstmate-work-handling, is the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."

findings.text: This card seems to contradict the capacity limit described in t2 and in "Counters". The caveat ("only a declared project capacity bounds it") appears only in claim c5 at the bottom of the page.
findings.source: ra3 card: "Isolated work is dispatched at once with no concurrency cap"

findings.text: The prerequisites are specific and usable. The header says one model does the work and a different one checks it, but only Claude Code is listed, so a reader can't tell whether a second model or provider is needed.
findings.source: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm (to install Claude Code)."
